findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order();` is added as an abstract method on a public SPI interface. Any third-party or custom CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface will fail to compile, and will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` while sorting. A `default int order() { return 0; }` would keep compatibility. The in-tree providers would then only need to override it with their own values.

findings.title: Providers with equal order are chosen silently, replacing the previous fail-fast error
findings.body: The old 'Multiple crypto providers' IllegalStateException is removed. Providers are now sorted by order() and the first is taken. The in-tree providers (Default, Elytron, FIPS1402) all return 200. If two of them end up on the classpath, for example FIPS and default, the pick depends on ServiceLoader discovery order, because the sort is stable and the order values tie. A misconfigured deployment that used to fail fast now silently runs with the wrong crypto provider, which is a risk in FIPS setups. The 'Ignored crypto providers' message is logged only at debug level. Ties should be detected and rejected or warned about, or the ignored providers should be logged at warn.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The method returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the JDK's SUN provider and not a BouncyCastle provider. Code that uses `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` or the provider's name, for example the `Signature.getInstance(..., BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` pattern, will resolve to SUN. The javadoc contract says BouncyCastle, so the behaviour is misleading and undocumented. Other methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, so any call path that reaches them fails at runtime.

findings.title: Dead code: result of ASN1Encoder write calls discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create encoders, write r and s, and discard the results. The same encoding is repeated in the return statement. These are leftover no-op lines and should be removed.

findings.title: Test uses one default-size EC key for all algorithms and only checks a self round-trip
findings.body: A single key from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512 (a P-256 key in practice). The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore sign with a 256-bit curve, which produces 32-byte r and s. These are then padded to 48 or 66 bytes, so the truncation and padding paths for real P-384 and P-521 signatures are not exercised. The test also only compares round-trip equality of this provider's own encode and decode. It never checks against the JDK-produced DER or verifies the converted signature, and it has no negative cases such as malformed DER. Bugs in the ASN1Decoder, for example a zero-length INTEGER throwing a runtime NumberFormatException instead of IOException, would go undetected.
